summary:
Across 16 evals (87 iterations, 3 per eval, no failed iterations), three evals (negative-s3-lifecycle, negative-efs-throughput, negative-ec2-cpu-only) were should_trigger:false negatives — trigger correctly fired as "not applicable" in all three, and expected_output/assertions/quality/consistency were all marked skipped, so they contribute no comparative signal either way.

Trigger firing itself was 100% for both variants on all 13 remaining evals, so that dimension never differentiates the two.

Expected-output match rate: with_skill met the expected output at 100% (or very high) on most evals — io2-iops-saturation, gp3-throughput-saturation, latency-impairment-fis, latency-indeterminate-no-signal, snapshot-cleanup-safety, kms-attach-error, io2-quota-error, io2-ratio-error-translated, operational-review — while without_skill lagged notably on several of these, most sharply on operational-review (0/3 vs 3/3), snapshot-cleanup-safety (1/3 vs 3/3), io2-quota-error (1/3 vs 3/3), and cost-spike-breakdown (0/3 vs 2/3, though without_skill's run data there is largely null/inconclusive - cost_avg $0.00, runtime 0s, suggesting that variant may not have executed meaningfully in that eval). Instance-ebs-limit and modification-optimizing-not-stuck showed both variants at low/mid expected-output rates (2/3 and ≤1/3 respectively for both), and approval-only-on-card had both variants at 0/3 — an assertion/behavior pattern neither variant satisfies, suggesting the expected-output criterion itself may need review there. latency-indeterminate-no-signal is a case where without_skill (3/3, medium confidence) outperformed with_skill (3/3, high confidence) on expected-output tied, but assertions and quality diverged there (see below).

Per-assertion detail shows a mix: many assertions pass for both (e.g., "Throughput stated in MiB/s," "no ModifyVolume/DeleteSnapshot executed," "AWS KMS named") — these don't differentiate. Some always fail for both (e.g., "gp3 throughput per IOPS rule cited," "Impairment is named") — indicating a behavior or assertion gap common to both variants. Several assertions show a clear with_skill-passes/without_skill-fails pattern (e.g., snapshot-cleanup-safety's owner-review and Recycle Bin mentions, operational-review's full-report and severity-labeling checks, io2-quota-error's usage-reporting and intake-question checks, instance-ebs-limit's "volume headroom stated"). No assertion showed the reverse (without_skill passing where with_skill consistently failed), though many are flagged "flaky" (inconsistent pass/fail across the 3 runs for one or both variants), which tempers confidence in any single assertion's verdict.

Quality comparisons (LLM-judged, pairwise) are mixed and evaluated on a subset of evals (several marked pairs_skipped, especially for chat-task evals like modification-optimizing-not-stuck, cost-spike-breakdown, operational-review, approval-only-on-card, where 0 or 1 of 3 pairs were evaluated — too few to draw conclusions). Where evaluated: with_skill was favored more often in io2-iops-saturation (6 vs 5, close), instance-ebs-limit (3-0, small n=1 pair), latency-impairment-fis (7 vs 4), io2-quota-error (3-0, n=1), io2-ratio-error-translated (9 vs 1, more decisive). without_skill was favored more often in gp3-throughput-saturation (6 vs 2), latency-indeterminate-no-signal (11 vs 0, decisive), snapshot-cleanup-safety (2 vs 1, n=1), kms-attach-error (3 vs 1, with 5 comparable). Confidence on these quality judgments is generally medium.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was consistently faster and cheaper on chat-task evals, often substantially (e.g., kms-attach-error 8s/$0.07 vs 13s/$0.11; io2-quota-error 9s/$0.08 vs 24s/$0.20; approval-only-on-card 9s/$0.08 vs 39s/$0.33; operational-review was an exception, with without_skill slightly slower at 2m2s vs 1m47s). On investigation-task evals, runtimes were closer and mixed (with_skill faster in gp3-throughput-saturation, latency-impairment-fis; without_skill faster in io2-iops-saturation; with_skill notably faster in latency-indeterminate-no-signal, 1m39s vs 2m17s). Several runtime comparisons flagged runs exceeding a 30s threshold, more often on gp3-throughput-saturation (all 3 pairs) and instance-ebs-limit (1 pair), with medium confidence.

Output consistency across repeated runs was generally "consistent" to "mostly_consistent" for both variants in most evals, meaning outputs were fairly stable run-to-run. Notable exceptions: in latency-indeterminate-no-signal, with_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.0) while without_skill was "mostly_consistent" (2.25) — a meaningful stability gap favoring without_skill there, and it aligns with without_skill's quality edge on that same eval. In io2-iops-saturation, with_skill was "consistent" (3.0) vs without_skill "mostly_consistent" (2.25).

Overall, the picture is a set of tradeoffs rather than a uniform pattern: with_skill tends to meet expected-output and assertion criteria more often across more evals, and wins quality comparisons on several evals, but runs longer and costs more on most chat tasks, and in one eval (latency-indeterminate-no-signal) showed both lower output consistency and lower quality-comparison results than without_skill. Several dimensions (quality on chat evals, some assertions) had limited sample sizes or flakiness that reduce confidence in those specific findings, and three evals contributed no comparative data due to being correctly-skipped negative triggers.

io2-iops-saturation.summary:
Both variants were evaluated on the same investigation task (3 runs each) looking at diagnosing an EBS/EC2 IOPS-throughput binding-layer issue.

Trigger and expected output: The behavior under test fired in all runs (3/3), and both variants met the expected output 3/3 times. Confidence in that expected-output judgment was "high" for with_skill and only "medium" for without_skill, meaning the expected-output match itself is on slightly less solid footing for without_skill even though the pass rate is identical.

Assertions (18 checks across 6 distinct assertion types, repeated over 3 runs): with_skill passed 14/18 (78%) and without_skill passed 11/18 (61%). Breaking this down:
- Two assertions always passed for both variants (judging the io2 volume by IOPS not throughput-percentage, and stating throughput in MiB/s) and one more (no ModifyVolume reported as executed) also passed 3/3 for both — these do not differentiate the variants.
- One assertion (comparing summed IOPS/throughput against instance baseline before naming the binding layer) was flaky but identical for both: 2/3 for each.
- One assertion ("binding layer is reported," a regex check) was flaky and favored with_skill (2/3) over without_skill (0/3).
- One assertion (giving an exact target IOPS presented as a proposal, not an executed change) was weak for both but worse for without_skill: with_skill 1/3 vs without_skill 0/3. This suggests this specific behavior is under-performing in both, more so in without_skill.

So of the differentiating assertions, with_skill passed more often; several other checks were a wash (both strong or both weak).

Quality comparison (3 pairs only — a small sample): overall ratings were close, with with_skill favored in 6 sub-ratings, without_skill favored in 5, and 1 comparable, at medium average confidence. Per criterion this splits unevenly: root_cause_accuracy leaned slightly toward without_skill (2 vs 1), while key_findings_accuracy and supporting_evidence_quality leaned slightly toward with_skill (2 vs 1 each), and impact_analysis_accuracy was split evenly. Given only 3 pairs, these differences are small in absolute terms and should be read as a rough signal, not a strong one.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~5m3s and $2.52 per run; without_skill averaged ~5m32s and $2.76 — with_skill was modestly faster (~29s) and cheaper (~$0.24) on average. Neither variant exceeded the runtime threshold in any of the 3 evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was low for both (with_skill 10.2%, without_skill 7.1%), with no compactions for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs: with_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0, high confidence) across all four measured dimensions. without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" (score 2.25, medium confidence), consistent on only 1 of 4 dimensions and "mostly consistent" on the other 3 — indicating somewhat more run-to-run variation in without_skill's outputs.

Overall picture: trigger firing and basic expected-output success were equivalent for both. Several assertions were identical (either both strong or both weak), but on the assertions that did differentiate the variants, with_skill passed more often, particularly on reporting the binding layer explicitly and on presenting IOPS recommendations as proposals. Quality ratings from the small 3-pair comparison were close to a wash, with a slight edge split across different criteria. with_skill also ran modestly faster, cheaper, and was more consistent across repeated runs, while without_skill showed more run-to-run variability and lower confidence in its expected-output match. These are moderate differences rather than a one-sided result, and the quality and assertion samples are small, so the findings should be treated as directional rather than conclusive.

gp3-throughput-saturation.summary:
Both variants were evaluated on an EBS/gp3 throughput investigation task across 3 runs each.

Trigger & expected output: The behavior under test fired in all runs (3/3), and both variants met the expected output in all 3 runs with high confidence — this dimension shows no difference between them and is a strong, high-confidence result for both.

Assertions (15 total checks): without_skill passed 10/15 (67%) vs with_skill 9/15 (60%) — a modest difference of one assertion. Breaking this down by individual assertion is more informative than the aggregate:
- Two assertions always passed for both variants (independence of gp3 IOPS/throughput provisioning with correct binding-dimension identification; throughput stated in MiB/s) — these aren't distinguishing the variants.
- One assertion always failed for both variants (citing the specific gp3 throughput-per-IOPS rule) — this indicates a shared gap or an assertion that may need rework, not a difference between variants.
- The instance EBS baseline check passed 3/3 for both, though confidence was medium for without_skill vs high for with_skill on that one.
- The clearest difference was on the assertion checking whether the proposed throughput target respects the gp3 0.25 MiB/s-per-IOPS rule: without_skill passed 1/3, with_skill passed 0/3. Both are low absolute pass rates (flagged as "flaky") and both skew toward failure, so this is a shared weakness, with without_skill only marginally better.

Quality comparison (3 pairs evaluated, judged at medium confidence): across 12 criterion-level comparisons, without_skill was favored 6 times, with_skill 2 times, and 4 were comparable. This leans toward without_skill producing somewhat higher-rated output on this small sample, particularly on supporting_evidence_quality and key_findings_accuracy, but with only 3 pairs and medium confidence, this should be read as a directional signal rather than a firm conclusion.

Runtime and cost: without_skill averaged 4m14s and $2.11; with_skill averaged 5m11s and $2.58 — without_skill was faster (~57s less) and cheaper (~$0.47 less) on average. All 3 runs in the runtime comparison exceeded the defined 30s threshold for both variants, so this threshold wasn't informative for distinguishing them. modification-optimizing-not-stuck.summary:
This eval tested a chat scenario about EBS volume modification status (whether a "stuck" modification is actually in a normal "optimizing" state, and related rules about modification limits/cooldowns). The triggering behavior fired in all 3 runs for both variants.

Expected output match was low for both variants and should be read with caution: with_skill met the expected output in 1/3 runs (33%, medium confidence) and without_skill in 0/3 runs (0%, but reported with high confidence). Neither variant reliably produced the fully expected response, with without_skill failing all three attempts.

Looking at the finer-grained per-assertion results (18 checks total, 6 distinct assertions x 3 runs each): with_skill passed 16/18 (89%) and without_skill passed 12/18 (67%). Breaking this down:
- Two assertions passed consistently for both variants (always_passes): stating the modification is not stuck, and explaining that the optimizing state already applies the new config. These don't differentiate the variants.
- One assertion (naming the optimizing state) also always passed for both.
- One assertion ("4 modifications per 24 hours rule is stated") was flaky for both and mostly failed: with_skill got it 1/3, without_skill 0/3 — suggesting this specific fact is rarely surfaced by either variant and may indicate a weak spot in the underlying behavior or prompt rather than a meaningful variant difference.
- Two assertions showed a gap favoring with_skill: "instance ceiling reported as separate finding" (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 1/3, medium confidence) and "no cooldown between modifications claimed" (with_skill 3/3 vs without_skill 2/3). These are the main places where the variants diverge.

Quality comparison data was not usable: all 3 pairs were skipped and none evaluated, so no direct quality-head-to-head judgment is available.

On runtime and cost, with_skill took about 24s and $0.20 per run on average, while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper at about 7s and $0.06. Context window utilization was low for both (6.1% vs 4.5%) with no compaction needed in either case. This represents a clear efficiency advantage for without_skill, alongside with_skill's edge on assertion pass rates — a tradeoff rather than a one-sided result.

Output consistency was rated "mostly_consistent" for both variants across repeated runs, with with_skill scoring slightly higher (2.67 vs 2.0 on the underlying scale) and high confidence in both assessments; with_skill had two dimensions rated fully "consistent" plus one "mostly_consistent," while without_skill had all three dimensions at "mostly_consistent."

Overall: with_skill shows higher expected-output match and assertion pass rates (particularly on the instance-ceiling and cooldown claims) and slightly more consistent outputs, while without_skill is substantially faster and cheaper. Both variants struggle with the same specific assertion (the 4-modifications-per-24-hours rule), and the overall expected-output pass rate is low for both, meaning the core task is not being fully satisfied by either variant. No direct quality comparison was available to weigh against these differences.

Expected-output match (high confidence on both sides): with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%), while without_skill met it in only 1 of 3 runs (33%). This is a sizable, high-confidence gap.

Assertion-level detail (27 assertions total) reinforces this: with_skill passed 25/27 (93%) vs without_skill's 11/27 (41%). Looking at individual assertions rather than the aggregate:
- Two assertions passed for both variants regardless of run (AMI-backing snapshot marked "Do not delete"; deletion described as a manual customer step) — these aren't differentiating since both handle them fine.
- Four assertions were passed consistently by with_skill but failed consistently by without_skill: flagging the ownerless/AMI-less snapshot for owner review, checking sharing/DLM tags directly rather than inferring, noting snapshots are incremental so savings are an upper bound, and naming "owner review" explicitly, and mentioning Recycle Bin for reversibility. These point to specific content/behavior gaps in without_skill's responses on this task.
- One assertion ("source volume still exists -> marked Verify") was flaky for without_skill (2/3) vs consistent for with_skill (3/3), with without_skill's confidence here rated medium (slightly weaker signal).
- One assertion ran in the opposite direction: "No DeleteSnapshot call reported as executed" passed 3/3 for without_skill but only 1/3 for with_skill — the only assertion where without_skill outperformed with_skill. This is worth flagging on its own since it's the one place the two variants' typical ranking reverses.

Quality comparison data is thin: only 1 of 3 pairs could be evaluated head-to-head (2 skipped), and that one comparison favored without_skill on accuracy and actionability but favored with_skill on completeness, with only medium confidence overall. Given only one comparable pair, this should be read as a weak, limited-sample signal rather than a firm conclusion, and it does not obviously line up with the much larger expected-output/assertion gap favoring with_skill.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged ~40s and $0.34 per run; without_skill averaged ~16s and $0.13 per run — without_skill was substantially faster and cheaper (about 24s less and $0.21 less per run), with neither exceeding the 30s runtime threshold in the one comparable runtime pair. Context window utilization was low for both (6.8% vs 4.8%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency was essentially identical between the two: both rated "mostly_consistent" overall with the same score (2.67) and the same dimension breakdown (2 consistent, 1 mostly consistent), both at high confidence — so run-to-run stability is not a differentiator here.

Overall picture: with_skill more reliably satisfied the detailed task requirements (expected output and most individual assertions, including several content-specific checks like tag verification, incremental-savings framing, and Recycle Bin mention), while without_skill was notably faster and cheaper and uniquely consistent on avoiding reporting an executed DeleteSnapshot call.
